question: Assuming Gareth Evan's Generality Constraint, if I understand a proposition Fa, should I be able to understand Fx (\forall x)? Assume I understand universal quantification.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes. On Evans' picture understanding a singular predicative thought Fa isn't just a brute primitive association between a particular mode of presentation of a and the predicate F; the mode of presentation you are using for a in Fa has to be one you could in principle redeploy. That is the Generality Constraint: if you think of a as F you are thinking of a under a concept that is possessed generally, not as an idiosyncratic tag tied to that one individual.

If F is possessed generally you can entertain the thought of F applying to objects in the domain in that very way. In particular you can entertain the schema ‘x is F’ with an arbitrary x in the same mode of presentation you employed for a. Since we are stipulating that you do understand the universal quantifier, combining that quantificational competence with general possession of F gives you competence for the closed thought ∀x Fx.

So having secure understanding of Fa together with understood ‘∀’ is just understanding the general deployment of F you are already committed to by the Generality Constraint. The particular instance Fa is thus a limiting case of, and is intelligible only against the background of, the general thought ∀x Fx.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes. On Evans’ reading the Generality Constraint is a constraint on the concepts you are using in a singular thought, not just on the particular singular proposition you happen to entertain. To understand that a is F you must understand F in a way that is not essentially tied to a. That is, you must grasp F as a property that can be applied to objects in general, and you must be able to think of an arbitrary object as possibly falling under F. 

Given that understanding, the conceptual content of F is already in your possession as a general concept. Since you are assumed to understand universal quantification, you can then combine that general grasp of F with the quantifier to get the thought that F holds of everything in the domain. Being able to think of any object as F under the Generality Constraint just is being able to entertain the general thought ∀x Fx; the particular instance Fa is only intelligible as an instance of that general mode of presentation.

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes. On Evans’s view to think/singularly understand Fa one must already be in possession of a general way of thinking about F, not merely a mode of presentation tied to the particular object a. The generality constraint is precisely that singular employment of a concept presupposes general employment of that concept. Once F is available to you in a way that can be detached from a, the thought is essentially that of an Fs of the form Fx, with x standing for the individual in general. Given that you are assumed to understand universal quantification, having the general concept F in your repertoire is enough to be able to grasp the quantificational articulation of that concept, ∀x Fx. Understanding Fa therefore entails being able to entertain F in its general form, and with the quantificational apparatus at hand that general form is manifest as the universal generalization.

3.text:
The Generality Constraint is not a logical entailment from Fa to ∀xFx and it is not a commitment to the truth of the universal generalisation.

On Evans's view to think / to understand that a is F is to think of a under the concept F. To be able to think of a under F is to be able to think of F as a property that can be applied to things in general. That is the capacity to entertain the open sentence Fx for an arbitrary x and, in particular, to entertain Fx for any x you can think of. That is what is required for the thought that a is F to be generalizable at all.

∀xFx is a closed, substantive claim about the extension of F. It says that F holds of every object in the domain. Understanding Fa gives you no standing to assert, and Evans does not require you to understand or accept, that universal claim. The constraint is about the generality of the mode of presentation of F, not about the truth of a universally quantified proposition about F.

If you do independently understand quantification you could, in principle, close the open schema Fx by means of the quantifier and form the sentence ∀xFx. That is a purely syntactic fact about your competence with quantification. It is not a requirement imposed by the Generality Constraint on your understanding of the singular proposition Fa. Understanding Fa requires a grasp of F as applicable in general, i.e. the schema Fx, not the understanding or acceptance of ∀xFx.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes. On Evans’ reading the Generality Constraint is a constraint on concept possession. To understand and entertain the singular thought Fa you have to possess the concept F and be able to apply it, and you have to possess the singular concept of a. Possession of a concept in Evans’ sense is possession of it as a general, typeable item: if you can deploy F in the particular case Fa you must be able to deploy F generically, i.e. to think of x is F as a deployable schema with the singular term replaced by a variable.

Given that I am assumed to understand universal quantification, being able to deploy the schema Fx is just being able to close it off with the quantifier. The general thought that the concept F is available for arbitrary application is exactly the thought that one can entertain ∀x Fx. So understanding Fa on Evans’ picture already commits me to having the general concept F available, and with the assumed competence with ‘∀’ that availability is the ability to understand the universal generalisation ∀x Fx. The constraint therefore requires the move from the particular attribution to the general form.

2.text:
The Generality Constraint is a condition on the possession and use of singular modes of presentation, not on the unrestricted use of the predicate F.

On Evans' view to think of an object a in the thought that Fa is to be in possession of a mode of presentation m of a which can be deployed with any concept that the thinker possesses. In effect

If S can think m is F

then S must be able to think m is G for every G in S's conceptual repertoire, and in particular S must be able to think general thoughts in which m occurs, e.g. thoughts of the form

∀x [ x is m → Fx ],  m = a → G(a), etc.

That is the generality that is required for m to be a genuine conceptually articulated way of thinking of a. It is generality with respect to the singular term a / m, not generality with respect to the open sentence Fx.

Possession of the predicate F is a separate matter. Possessing F is what enables Fa to be thought at all. If S really possesses F and S also possesses the quantifier ∀, S can form the thought ∀x Fx, but that is a further exercise of the concepts F and ∀. The Generality Constraint about singular thought does not license the move

Fa  →  ∀x Fx

and it does not require the thinker who can think Fa to be able to assess the truth of, or even to understand, the unrestricted generalisation ∀x Fx about the extension of F. Understanding Fa only commits you to being able to think a under the same mode of presentation with other predicates you possess, i.e. to being able to think G(a) for any G you possess, and to think the a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx]. It does not commit you to knowing whether F holds for every object in the domain.

In the usual formulation this is stated with the a-generalisation rather than ∀x Fx. If that is what is meant, i.e. ∀x[x=a → Fx], then yes: the Generality Constraint does require that a thinker who can think Fa be able to think the general thought about a. For the unrestricted ∀x Fx the Constraint gives no such requirement.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes. On Evans' picture the constraint is a requirement of systematicity on the thinker's conceptual repertoire. Grasping a singular thought that a is F essentially involves grasping the property F as a mode of presentation that can be applied to objects. If you really understand the thought Fa you understand F qua property, not merely as a tag attached to a particular token a, because otherwise the thought would be an isolated, non-substitutable item in your mental economy. Evans is precisely ruling out that kind of isolation: a thinkable particular must be thinkable under a concept that is available for recombination.

Given that you are assumed to understand universal quantification, the only remaining ingredient for ∀x Fx is the concept F itself. Since understanding Fa already gives you F in the only way Evans lets it be given, the Generality Constraint demands that you be able to deploy F in a general schema. In other words, the ability to think Fa commits you to being able to think the general thought Fx for an arbitrary x, and with quantificational competence in hand that is just the thought ∀x Fx. So the constraint does entail that from understanding Fa you should be able to understand the generalization, modulo the background quantificational understanding we are stipulating.

6.text:
The Generality Constraint is a constraint on conceptual competence and on the form
in which thoughts are entertained, not on what a subject happens to believe.

If you are in a position to entertain a thought of the form

  Fa

with the concept F applied to the particular object a, you cannot be in
possession of F in a way which is essentially tied to a. To possess the
concept F at all is to possess it in a way which is usable salva
conceptu with other arguments and which is governed by a rule of
substitution for the argument place. That is what it is for F to be a
genuinely general concept.

In Evans’s terms you must be able to think the thought in the format
`x is F` - i.e. to entertain the open sentence Fx - and to move inferentially
with it. Possession of F is the possession of the ability to substitute
different terms for the argument place, to combine F with a variable,
to form conditionals, negations, etc. with F, and in general to engage
in the normal inferential activity associated with a concept. On that
basis you have the conceptual resources to parse the linguistic item
∀x Fx and, given independent mastery of the universal quantifier, you
understand what it would say to ascribe F to every x.

That is not the same as understanding, and still less as being committed
to, the substantive proposition ∀x Fx. The Generality Constraint gives you
the schema Fx and the ability to form the closed form ∀x Fx from it
once you understand ∀. It does not give you the truth of the
generalisation, nor does it imply that Fa entails ∀x Fx. The universal
proposition is a further, world-involving claim about the extension of F.
Understanding Fa gives you the general concept F, and with that the
competence to understand Fx as a variable governed thought and hence,
in principle, to understand the sentence ∀x Fx. The constraint says
nothing about whether you do in fact accept the universal claim.

10.text:
The Generality Constraint is a constraint on the mode of presentation of the
property, not on the content of the belief you have about a.

If a subject can think the singular thought that a is F the thought must
contain a general concept F for the subject. To have the concept F for the
subject is to be able to deploy F in thought independently of a, i.e. to be
able to entertain the schema

    x is F

for an arbitrary x in the subject's domain of discourse, and hence to be
able to think of a as falling under the same general mode of presentation
that could be applied to other objects. That is the generality that Evans
requires.

That generality is the ability to think Fx with x free/arbitrary, not the
ability to think the closed universal proposition

    ∀x Fx

The closed universal is a quite different proposition with the content
that every object in the domain is F. Understanding Fa gives you a
general concept F and a fact about a, it gives you no information at all
about the F-status of other objects, and certainly does not make you in
a position to grasp the truth-conditions of ∀x Fx. The ability to form the
syntactic string ∀x Fx follows only from the fact that you understand
universal quantification and you now have the general concept F. In the
sense of being able to parse and form the sentence that is available, but
that is not the semantic understanding of the universal claim which
Evans' constraint is meant to secure. The constraint secures only that F
is a generalisable concept, i.e. that you can think Fx for an arbitrary x,
and therefore can think about F generally. It does not entail that you
can understand, let alone believe, that F holds of everything.

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: No, not the universal claim ∀x Fx.

The Generality Constraint is a constraint on the possession of concepts, not a logic of entailment from a particular instance to a universal.

If you genuinely think / understand Fa you must already grasp F as a general concept. Evans requires that the mode of presentation under which you think of a be a mode which you can deploy with a variable. That is, possession of the concept F requires being able to entertain the general schema ‘x is F’ and, on demand, to think of an arbitrary object as falling under F. It requires you to be able to think of a in a way that generalises, e.g. that you can think ‘x is F’, ‘x = a → Fx’, ‘there is an x such that Fx’, etc.

That is not the same as understanding, let alone being committed to, the closed quantified claim ∀x Fx. ∀x Fx is a substantive proposition about the extension of F in the world. Understanding the open schema Fx and understanding the quantifier ∀x is enough to syntactically grasp the sentence ∀x Fx, but Fa plus GC gives you no reason to think ∀x Fx is true, and GC does not demand that you do. The constraint is that F be projectible from a to variable positions, not that you infer the universal generalisation from the particular instance a.

In the usual formulation the requirement is for the general form with a free variable, ‘x is F’, not for the universal generalisation ∀x Fx. So GC gives you general grasp of F, not a commitment to all things being F.

8.text:
Under Evans a mode of presentation is grasped only if it is projectible. To think Fa in a way that is genuinely about a under the mode `F' is to have the concept F in the thinker’s possession independently of the particular object a.

That is what the Generality Constraint demands: the way you are able to think of a as F must be a way you can think of *any* object as F. In particular the concept F must be available to you as a function from individuals to truth values, i.e. as the schema `x is F' . If you could think `a is F' only as a piece of information essentially tied to a, you would not have F as a concept at all.

So far as intelligibility is concerned you must be able to entertain the open sentence Fx with a free variable, and to recombine it with other concepts. If in addition you understand universal quantification you can then entertain the quantified sentence ∀x Fx as a well formed thought whose constituent mode of presentation is the same F you already grasp in Fa. Understanding Fa does not give you any warrant for believing ∀x Fx, and it does not entail that you can decide its truth, but it does entail that the thought is intelligible to you, because F is already possessed as a generally deployable concept.

That is the content of the constraint: singular thought presupposes general thought, and the particular instance Fa presupposes the grasp of the general form Fx, and with a grasp of ∀, the grasp of ∀x Fx.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes. 

On Evans's picture the ability to think a singular thought Fa is not a self-contained act with a name 'a' glued on top of a concept F. To understand Fa at all is to grasp F as a general mode of presentation that can be entertained with different terms in its argument place. The Generality Constraint is that if you can think of a as falling under F, you must be able to think of F with a free variable in place of a, i.e. you must be able to entertain the general thought Fx. That is a requirement on the content of your thought about a: the concept F is only intelligible for you as general.

Once you can entertain Fx, and given the stipulation that you understand universal quantification, you can close that general thought under the universal quantifier. Understanding the quantifier is understanding the rule by which a general open formula Fx is transformed into the closed general proposition ∀x Fx. So possession of the singular thought Fa together with competence with ∀ entails possession of the quantified thought ∀x Fx. In Evans's terms, the singular thought is posterior to the general concept; you cannot have the former without already having the conceptual resources for the latter, and with universal quantification in place those resources deliver the universal generalisation.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes, modulo the usual Evansian qualification. 

The Generality Constraint is a constraint on the format of the contents a thinker can have, not on the truth conditions she knows. If you can genuinely think the atomic singular thought Fa you have to be in possession of the property concept F in a way that is not essentially tied to the particular token a. To think Fa at all is to have a way of thinking of F which can in principle be applied to whatever can be substituted for a.

In Evans’ jargon the mental mode of presentation of F that underlies your understanding of Fa must be generalizable. It has to be the same mode of presentation that would underlie the open thought Fx with x free. If the mode of presentation of F that you deploy for a were essentially singular and non-generalizable, then Fa would be an essentially token-reflexive thought and you could not think of a under the concept F at all. That is what the Generality Constraint rules out.

Once you have that general mode of presentation of F, and you are assumed to understand universal quantification, the universal closure of the open formula is in principle intelligible to you. It is not required by the Constraint that you know whether ∀x Fx is true, nor that you be able to evaluate it, just that you are able to recognize what the general proposition ∀x Fx says and to embed Fx in general thoughts about F. The atomic Fa is intelligible only on the condition that you can understand the general concept F that is being predicated of a, i.e. you can understand Fx and, with quantification in place, ∀x Fx.

12.text:
Under Evans the content of a singular thought is fixed by the general
concept under which the object is thought of. 

To think/understand that a is F is to deploy F as a concept that is
applicable to objects in the thinker's conceptual scheme. It is not a
primitive, object- and occasion-bound notion of F that is only ever
available in the form `...a...`. On the Generality Constraint a
concept that can be entertained in the singular can be entertained
in the general. If you can think the thought Fa you must have grasped
F as a property/ predicate which you can apply wherever you can think
of an object, i.e. you can think the open thought 
Fx, and you can think Fa as the instance x=a of that general
thought.

Possession of the general concept F is the only conceptual
requirement for entertaining a universally quantified thought with F
as matrix. If, as stipulated, universal quantification is already
in your grasp, then the combination `∀` + F is a meaningful thought
in your repertoire. You can therefore entertain the proposition
∀x Fx as a proposition about F, just as you can entertain ∃x Fx or
x is F for an arbitrary x.

That does not entail that understanding Fa gives you warrant for,
or knowledge that, ∀x Fx is true. The Generality Constraint is a
constraint on conceptual possession and the form of entertainability,
not on empirical knowledge about the extension of F. You may be in a
position to understand the quantified content while being in no
position to know its truth value. It is the generalizability of the
predicate that the constraint secures, and in that sense you do get
from Fa to the general schema Fx and, with a grasp of ∀, to the
closed quantified form ∀x Fx.

Understanding the open schema Fx and understanding the quantifier ∀x is enough to syntactically grasp the sentence ∀x Fx, but Fa plus GC gives you no reason to think ∀x Fx is true, and GC does not demand that you do. The constraint is that F be projectible from a to variable positions, not that you infer the universal generalisation from the particular instance a.

In the usual formulation the requirement is for the general form with a free variable, ‘x is F’, not for the universal generalisation ∀x Fx. So GC gives you general grasp of F, not a commitment to all things being F.
public_text.8:
Under Evans a mode of presentation is grasped only if it is projectible. To think Fa in a way that is genuinely about a under the mode `F' is to have the concept F in the thinker’s possession independently of the particular object a.

That is what the Generality Constraint demands: the way you are able to think of a as F must be a way you can think of *any* object as F. In particular the concept F must be available to you as a function from individuals to truth values, i.e. as the schema `x is F' . If you could think `a is F' only as a piece of information essentially tied to a, you would not have F as a concept at all.

So far as intelligibility is concerned you must be able to entertain the open sentence Fx with a free variable, and to recombine it with other concepts. If in addition you understand universal quantification you can then entertain the quantified sentence ∀x Fx as a well formed thought whose constituent mode of presentation is the same F you already grasp in Fa. Understanding Fa does not give you any warrant for believing ∀x Fx, and it does not entail that you can decide its truth, but it does entail that the thought is intelligible to you, because F is already possessed as a generally deployable concept.

That is the content of the constraint: singular thought presupposes general thought, and the particular instance Fa presupposes the grasp of the general form Fx, and with a grasp of ∀, the grasp of ∀x Fx.
public_text.14:
Yes. 

On Evans's picture the ability to think a singular thought Fa is not a self-contained act with a name 'a' glued on top of a concept F. To understand Fa at all is to grasp F as a general mode of presentation that can be entertained with different terms in its argument place. The Generality Constraint is that if you can think of a as falling under F, you must be able to think of F with a free variable in place of a, i.e. you must be able to entertain the general thought Fx. That is a requirement on the content of your thought about a: the concept F is only intelligible for you as general.

Once you can entertain Fx, and given the stipulation that you understand universal quantification, you can close that general thought under the universal quantifier. Understanding the quantifier is understanding the rule by which a general open formula Fx is transformed into the closed general proposition ∀x Fx. So possession of the singular thought Fa together with competence with ∀ entails possession of the quantified thought ∀x Fx. In Evans's terms, the singular thought is posterior to the general concept; you cannot have the former without already having the conceptual resources for the latter, and with universal quantification in place those resources deliver the universal generalisation.
public_text.4:
Yes, modulo the usual Evansian qualification. 

The Generality Constraint is a constraint on the format of the contents a thinker can have, not on the truth conditions she knows. If you can genuinely think the atomic singular thought Fa you have to be in possession of the property concept F in a way that is not essentially tied to the particular token a. To think Fa at all is to have a way of thinking of F which can in principle be applied to whatever can be substituted for a.

In Evans’ jargon the mental mode of presentation of F that underlies your understanding of Fa must be generalizable. It has to be the same mode of presentation that would underlie the open thought Fx with x free. If the mode of presentation of F that you deploy for a were essentially singular and non-generalizable, then Fa would be an essentially token-reflexive thought and you could not think of a under the concept F at all. That is what the Generality Constraint rules out.

Once you have that general mode of presentation of F, and you are assumed to understand universal quantification, the universal closure of the open formula is in principle intelligible to you. It is not required by the Constraint that you know whether ∀x Fx is true, nor that you be able to evaluate it, just that you are able to recognize what the general proposition ∀x Fx says and to embed Fx in general thoughts about F. The atomic Fa is intelligible only on the condition that you can understand the general concept F that is being predicated of a, i.e. you can understand Fx and, with quantification in place, ∀x Fx.

Under Evans the content of a singular thought is fixed by the general
concept under which the object is thought of. 

To think/understand that a is F is to deploy F as a concept that is
applicable to objects in the thinker's conceptual scheme. It is not a
primitive, object- and occasion-bound notion of F that is only ever
available in the form `...a...`. On the Generality Constraint a
concept that can be entertained in the singular can be entertained
in the general. If you can think the thought Fa you must have grasped
F as a property/ predicate which you can apply wherever you can think
of an object, i.e. you can think the open thought 
Fx, and you can think Fa as the instance x=a of that general
thought.

Possession of the general concept F is the only conceptual
requirement for entertaining a universally quantified thought with F
as matrix. If, as stipulated, universal quantification is already
in your grasp, then the combination `∀` + F is a meaningful thought
in your repertoire. You can therefore entertain the proposition
∀x Fx as a proposition about F, just as you can entertain ∃x Fx or
x is F for an arbitrary x.

That does not entail that understanding Fa gives you warrant for,
or knowledge that, ∀x Fx is true. The Generality Constraint is a
constraint on conceptual possession and the form of entertainability,
not on empirical knowledge about the extension of F. You may be in a
position to understand the quantified content while being in no
position to know its truth value. It is the generalizability of the
predicate that the constraint secures, and in that sense you do get
from Fa to the general schema Fx and, with a grasp of ∀, to the
closed quantified form ∀x Fx.

Key shared background:

Possession of F therefore requires being able to entertain the open schema ‘x is F’ for an arbitrary x, i.e. to deploy F with a free variable, to substitute different terms for the argument place, and to recombine F inferentially. That is the projectibility / generalizability that Evans requires.

Disagreement is about closure under ∀:
* Yes camp: 1,4,5,7,8,13,14. Understanding Fa already gives you F in the general mode required by GC. With independent grasp of ∀ you therefore have the conceptual resources for the closed form ∀x Fx. The particular Fa is intelligible only against the background of the general concept F, and with quantificational competence that background is manifest as understanding of ∀x Fx. Some phrase this as the singular thought being posterior to the general concept.
* No / qualified camp: 10,11,2,3,6. GC secures only the open, generalisable schema Fx with x free/arbitrary, and more precisely the a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx] or generality with respect to the singular term a. It does not secure the substantive content that F holds of every object. ∀x Fx is a world-involving claim about the extension of F; understanding Fa gives you a general concept F and a fact about a, but no information about other objects, and no warrant to grasp the truth-conditions of the universal. With quantifier competence you can parse/form the syntactic string ∀x Fx, but semantic understanding / acceptance of the universal claim is not required by GC and is not entailed by Fa.

Key nuances raised:
* Understanding vs warrant/ belief/ knowledge of truth. Several colleagues stress GC gives intelligibility / entertainability, not knowledge that ∀x Fx is true.
* Generality w.r.t predicate F vs generality w.r.t singular mode of presentation m of a. Colleague 2 stresses the classic formulation is generality of the singular term: if you can think m is F you must be able to think m is G for any G you possess, giving a-generalizations rather than unrestricted ∀x Fx.
* The open schema Fx is what GC directly requires; closure under ∀ is a further step that uses separate quantificational competence.

Unresolved for me: whether “be able to understand ∀x Fx” is meant as syntactic/semantic intelligibility of the quantified sentence given possession of F and ∀, or as a substantive commitment to the universal proposition. On the former, the Yes camp seems right; on the latter, the qualified No camp seems right. The stipulation “Assume I understand universal quantification” is doing heavy work and is interpreted differently by colleagues.

I will keep tracking the open-schema vs closed-universal distinction and the understanding vs warrant distinction in later rounds.
reflection_text.6:
The question is whether Evans’s Generality Constraint, plus stipulated competence with ∀, makes understanding Fa sufficient for being able to understand the general form, and in particular the closed universal ∀x Fx.

Core Evansian idea that recurs across colleagues: to think/understand Fa you must possess F as a general concept, not as a token-reflexive tag tied essentially to a. Possession of F is possession of a mode of presentation that can be detached from a and redeployed with other terms/arguments. That is the generality requirement.

Disagreement is about what 'generality' amounts to.

Yes / essentially yes camp: 1,4,5,7,8,9,12,13,14. Argument: singular thought is posterior to general concept. If you really grasp F in Fa you grasp F qua property that can be entertained with a free variable, i.e. the open schema Fx. With independent mastery of universal quantification the only remaining ingredient for ∀x Fx is the already-possessed general F, so the closed universal is intelligible in principle. Understanding Fa commits you to being able to think Fx for arbitrary x, and with ∀ in hand that is just understanding ∀x Fx as a meaningful thought. Several add the qualification that this is intelligibility/possession, not warrant or truth: GC does not give you knowledge that ∀x Fx is true, nor an entailment from Fa to ∀x Fx.

No / only open-schema camp: 10,11,3,2,6 with nuance. Argument: GC is a constraint on conceptual possession and mode of presentation of the property, not on the content of beliefs about the world. What GC secures is the ability to entertain the schema x is F with x free/arbitrary, and hence to think about F generally, not the ability to grasp the substantive closed proposition ∀x Fx that every object is F. Understanding Fa gives you a general concept F and a fact about a; it gives no information about other objects and does not make you in a position to grasp truth-conditions of ∀x Fx. Syntactic formation of ∀x Fx follows from having F + quantifier competence, but semantic understanding/acceptance of the universal claim is not required by GC. The constraint is about projectibility/generalizability of the predicate, not about inference from a particular instance to the universal generalisation.

Key nuance raised by Colleague 2: Evansian generality is often formulated with respect to the singular term a, e.g. ability to think m is G for any G, and the a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx], not unrestricted ∀x Fx. That is distinct from generality with respect to the open sentence Fx.

Unresolved/important distinctions to track:
* Intelligibility/ability to entertain vs warrant/belief/truth of ∀x Fx.
* Open schema Fx with free variable vs closed universal ∀x Fx.
* Generality with respect to the concept F vs generality with respect to the singular mode of presentation of a.
* GC as a condition on possession vs a logical entailment Fa → ∀x Fx.

My current working synthesis: GC requires possession of F in general form, i.e. ability to think Fx for an arbitrary x. Given stipulated quantifier competence, that general possession makes ∀x Fx intelligible/parasable as a thought you can entertain with the same mode of presentation of F used in Fa. GC does not entail that you believe, know, or have epistemic warrant for ∀x Fx, nor does it license the inference from Fa to ∀x Fx. The disagreement between colleagues is largely verbal about what counts as “understanding ∀x Fx”: mere conceptual intelligibility vs substantive semantic commitment to the universal claim.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think Colleagues 10, 11, 2 and 3 get the motivation of the Generality Constraint exactly right, and that’s why the conclusion they draw is too restrictive.

They are right that GC is a constraint on possession of a mode of presentation, not a licence to infer the truth of a universal generalisation from a singular instance. It does not give you warrant for, nor commitment to, believing that ∀x Fx is true. Understanding Fa does not give you information about the F-status of other objects.

Where I depart is on what it means to have F as a general concept once you also understand universal quantification. The constraint requires that if you can think Fa you must be able to deploy F independently of a, i.e. you must be able to entertain the schema x is F for an arbitrary x. That is not a merely syntactic ability to form a string with a free variable; it is a requirement that F be possessed as a genuinely general mode of presentation.

If F is possessed in that way, and you are stipulated to understand ∀, then the closed form ∀x Fx is already an intelligible articulation of the very same general possession. Possessing F generally just is possessing the conceptual resources to embed Fx under the quantifier you already grasp. Understanding ∀ is understanding what it is to close an open formula over a domain; combining that with general possession of F gives you the competence to entertain ∀x Fx as a content, to know what it would say to ascribe F to every x, even if you have no reason to assert or know that it is true.

So the Generality Constraint does not give you a doxastic commitment to ∀x Fx, and it certainly does not give you Fa → ∀x Fx. It does give you that Fa is intelligible only against the background of a general grasp of F, and with an independent grasp of ∀ that background is just the ability to understand the quantified content ∀x Fx. In that Evansian sense of understanding as being in a position to entertain a content on the basis of concept possession, yes: understanding Fa commits you to being able to understand ∀x Fx.

6.text:
Yes, in the sense of intelligibility/possession, not in the sense of warrant or entailment.

On Evans’ picture singular employment presupposes general possession. To think/understand Fa in a conceptually articulated way you must possess F as a mode of presentation that is not essentially tied to the token a. Possession of F is possession of F as a type that can be detached from a and redeployed with other arguments. That is just the ability to entertain the open schema Fx for an arbitrary x, and to think of a as the instance x=a of that general thought.

Possession of the general concept F is the only conceptual prerequisite for entertaining a quantified thought with F as matrix. With the stipulation that universal quantification is already understood, the combination ∀ + F is in your repertoire. You can therefore entertain the proposition ∀x Fx as a meaningful thought whose constituent mode of presentation of F is the same mode of presentation you already deploy in Fa.

That is not the same as Fa entailing ∀x Fx, nor does GC give you knowledge, belief or epistemic warrant for ∀x Fx. GC is a constraint on the format of contents you can have and on the form of entertainability, not on the extension of F in the world. You are in a position to understand what ∀x Fx says, to parse it and to use F generally, while remaining entirely agnostic about its truth. The universal generalisation is intelligible to you because Fa is intelligible only against the background of the general concept F, and with a grasp of ∀ that general background is manifest as ∀x Fx.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Yes.

On Evans the Generality Constraint is a constraint on concept possession and on the form in which a thought can be entertained, not on what you happen to believe about the extension of F.

To understand/understand that a is F you cannot be in possession of F in a way that is essentially tied to a. Possession of F has to be possession of F as a genuinely general, recombinable mode of presentation. That is what it is for F to be projectible: you must be able to entertain the schema x is F with an arbitrary x in the same mode of presentation you used for a, and to combine F with other concepts you possess.

If F is possessed in that general way, and we are stipulating that you do understand universal quantification, then the conceptual resources for the closed thought ∀x Fx are already in place. Understanding ∀ is understanding the rule by which an open, general thought Fx is closed under the universal quantifier. General possession of F gives you the matrix, quantificational competence gives you the closure operation. The particular instance Fa is intelligible only against the background of that general deployment of F, and with ∀ in hand that deployment is manifest as the universally quantified thought.

That does not commit you to believing or knowing that ∀x Fx is true, nor does it give you warrant for the generalisation from the particular instance. The Constraint is about intelligibility and possession, not about epistemic entitlement or truth. But it does require that the thought ∀x Fx be intelligible to you, because you already possess F generally and you already possess ∀. Singular understanding of Fa therefore presupposes the ability to understand the general form Fx and, with quantificational competence stipulated, the closed form ∀x Fx.

3.text:
On Evans the Generality Constraint is a constraint on possession of the concept F, not on the truth of what you think about a.

To think/singularly understand Fa at all you must possess F as a general, recombinable concept. That is possession of the open schema `x is F` with a free, arbitrary x: F is available to you independently of the particular token a, it can be substituted for different terms, combined with other concepts, negated, etc. The singular instance Fa is intelligible only as an instance of that general mode of presentation.

Possession of F in that general way is exactly what the Generality Constraint demands. It is not a logical entailment Fa ⊨ ∀x Fx and it does not give you warrant or knowledge that F holds of every object in the domain.

Given the stipulation that you understand universal quantification, that general possession of F is also the possession of the resources to close the schema under ∀. You can then parse, entertain and grasp the meaning of the closed proposition ∀x Fx and of other quantified forms ∃x Fx, ∀x[x=a → Fx], etc. That is intelligibility/possibility of understanding the sentence, not commitment to its truth.

So yes in the Evansian sense: understanding Fa commits you to being able to entertain Fx for an arbitrary x, and with quantifier competence in hand to being able to understand the universal quantification ∀x Fx as a proposition whose matrix is the same generally possessed F. No in the sense of commitment: GC does not require you to believe, know or be able to assess ∀x Fx; it secures the generalizability of F, not the truth of the unrestricted generalisation. The a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx] is the canonical formal expression of the required generality.

To understand Fa genuinely is to possess F as a concept that is not essentially tied to the particular token a. Possession of a concept in Evans’ sense is possession as a type, i.e. as a mode of presentation that is available for recombination with different arguments. That is the ability to entertain the general thought

x is F

for an arbitrary x in your domain, and to deploy F with substitution salva conceptu, to form conditionals, negations, etc. with F, and in general to have F as a generally projectible item in your mental economy.

If universal quantification is independently in your repertoire the only missing ingredient for the closed form ∀x Fx is the concept F itself. General possession of F together with competence with ∀ is competence to parse and grasp the content of the closed quantified sentence. You can entertain ∀x Fx as a proposition about F, just as you can entertain ∃x Fx or Fx for an arbitrary x. In that intelligibility/possession sense the singular thought commits you to being able to understand the general form and, with ∀ mastered, the universal closure of that form.

That is not a commitment to the truth of ∀x Fx, and it is not an entailment Fa ⊨ ∀x Fx. You may be in a position to understand what ∀x Fx says while being in no position to know whether it is true.

On the usual Evansian reading the most perspicuous generalisation secured by GC for the singular term is the a-generalisation ∀x[x = a → Fx], generality with respect to the singular mode of presentation of a. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The Evansian core is stable: to think/understand Fa you must possess F as a general, recombinable mode of presentation, not a token-reflexive tag tied essentially to a. Possession of F is possession of the ability to deploy F independently of a, i.e. to entertain the open schema Fx for an arbitrary x, to substitute terms for the argument place, and to combine F inferentially. Singular thought is posterior to general concept.

Round 1 largely converges on the intelligibility/warrant distinction that was already flagged. GC is a constraint on concept possession and the format in which a thought can be entertained, not a principle of inference Fa → ∀x Fx and not a source of warrant, knowledge or belief that F holds of everything. Understanding Fa gives you a general concept F and a fact about a; it gives no information about the F-status of other objects.

The current split is therefore verbal about what counts as “understanding ∀x Fx”.

Yes/intelligibility camp 1,10,11,12,13,14,5,6,7,9: General possession of F plus stipulated mastery of ∀ makes the closed form intelligible/parasable. Possessing F generally just is possessing the resources to embed Fx under the quantifier you already grasp. Understanding ∀ is understanding the rule that closes an open formula; with quantifier competence in hand the open schema Fx is systematically closable, so ∀x Fx is the same general mode of presentation exhibited in quantificational form. They stress this is possession/intelligibility, not endorsement: GC does not give warrant for, nor commitment to, the truth of ∀x Fx, and does not license inference from Fa to ∀x Fx.

No/open-schema camp 2,8 with nuance from 3,4,6: GC secures projectibility/free-variable entertainability of F, i.e. Fx with x free and, canonically, the a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx], generality with respect to the singular mode of presentation of a. The unrestricted closed universal ∀x Fx is a substantive world-involving claim about the extension of F. Understanding Fa gives you the general concept F and the ability to form the string ∀x Fx syntactically once ∀ is mastered, but GC does not require you to grasp, assess or be committed to the substantive content that every object is F. The requirement is for the schema, not the endorsement of the universal generalisation.

Persistent unresolved nuances:
* Intelligibility/ability to entertain vs warrant/belief/truth of ∀x Fx.
* Open schema Fx with free variable vs closed universal ∀x Fx.
* Generality with respect to the concept F vs generality with respect to the singular term a/m, i.e. a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx] vs unrestricted ∀x Fx.
* GC as condition on possession vs logical entailment Fa → ∀x Fx.

My working synthesis remains: GC requires possession of F in general form, i.e. ability to think Fx for an arbitrary x. Given stipulated quantifier competence, that general possession makes ∀x Fx intelligible as a meaningful content you can entertain with the same mode of presentation of F used in Fa. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The debate has converged around a nuanced distinction between intelligibility/possession and warrant/belief/truth.

The Generality Constraint is now widely described as a constraint on concept possession and on the format in which a thought can be entertained, not a principle of inference Fa → ∀x Fx and not a commitment to the truth or extension of F. To understand / think Fa on Evans is to possess F as a general, projectible, recombinable mode of presentation, not a tag essentially tied to a. Possession of F is possession of the open, variable-governed schema x is F, ability to substitute different terms for the argument place, to form conditionals, negations, etc. with F, and in particular to entertain the a-generalisation ∀x[x = a → Fx], x = a → G(a), etc. That is generality with respect to the concept F and, in Colleague 2’s formulation, generality with respect to the singular mode of presentation of a.

With that in place the dispute is whether, given the stipulation that I understand universal quantification, that general possession already yields intelligibility of the closed universal ∀x Fx.

Yes/intelligibility camp – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,4,5,6,7,9 – argue that understanding ∀ is understanding the operation of closing an open formula over a domain. General possession of F is the matrix for ∀x Fx. Once F is possessed as the schema Fx and ∀ is mastered, the closed form ∀x Fx is the same general mode of presentation made explicit by the quantificational apparatus. In that Evansian sense of being able to entertain a content, parse it, know what it would say to ascribe F to every x, understanding Fa commits me to being able to understand ∀x Fx as a meaningful thought about F, even though I may be agnostic about its truth. The particular instance is posterior to the general concept; systematicity requires that Fa be intelligible only against the background of a generally available F, and with ∀ in hand that background is manifest as the intelligibility of the universal form. No warrant, knowledge or belief that ∀x Fx is true is required.

No/nuanced camp – Colleagues 2,3,8, and parts of 10/11/4 – stress that GC secures only projectibility/free-variable entertainability, i.e. Fx with x free/arbitrary, and the a-generalisation ∀x[x = a → Fx]. Understanding Fa gives me a general concept F and a fact about a, but no information about the F-status of other objects and no semantic grasp of the truth-conditions of the substantive closed proposition ∀x Fx. That the string ∀x Fx can be syntactically formed from a generally possessed F plus mastered ∀ is trivial parsing competence, not the semantic understanding of the universal claim that every object is F. The substantive claim remains world-involving and is not entailed nor required by GC; GC is about the generality of the mode of presentation of F and of the singular term a, not an unrestricted claim about the extension of F.

Key distinctions I am retaining:
* open schema Fx with free/arbitrary variable vs closed quantified proposition ∀x Fx;
* intelligibility/possession/parsing vs doxastic commitment, warrant, knowledge of truth;
* generality with respect to predicate F vs generality with respect to singular term a / mode of presentation m, hence the canonical Evansian generalisation is the a-generalisation not the unrestricted universal.

Changes from earlier: I now see broad convergence that GC does not give epistemic commitment to ∀x Fx and does not licence Fa ⊢ ∀x Fx. The remaining live issue is the strength of the ‘understand ∀’ stipulation. If understanding ∀ is really understanding closure, then possession of the open schema plus ∀ competence arguably yields intelligibility of ∀x Fx as content. If understanding ∀ is taken more minimally, GC only requires the open projectible form.

Unresolved for me: whether Evans himself requires grasp of the unrestricted closed universal as a thought, or only the projectible open schema and a-generalisation. The textual emphasis on projectibility and singular-term generality points toward the latter, while the systematicity and ‘possession = ability to recombine with quantifiers’ line points toward the former in the weak intelligibility sense.

reflection_text.11:
The question is now largely about how to read “be able to understand ∀x Fx” – as intelligibility/possession vs epistemic warrant/acceptance of truth.

Stable background:
* GC is a constraint on concept possession / mode of presentation, not a logical entailment Fa → ∀x Fx.
* To genuinely think/understand Fa you must possess F as a general, projectible concept, not as a tag tied essentially to a. Possession of F requires ability to entertain the open schema ‘x is F’ for an arbitrary x, substitute different terms, recombine inferentially. Singular employment presupposes general employment.

Current convergence from round 1:
* Most colleagues now accept a qualified Yes. 1,10,11,12,13,14,5,6,7,3,4 say: GC gives you general possession of F; with stipulated competence with ∀ you have the conceptual resources to entertain/parses the closed form ∀x Fx as a meaningful content. Understanding Fa therefore commits you to being able to understand, in Evansian intelligibility/possession sense, ∀x Fx.
* The same colleagues stress this is not warrant, belief, knowledge or entailment. GC does not give you reason to think ∀x Fx is true, does not make you committed to the extension claim, does not license inference from a particular to universal. Projectibility ≠ truth.

Persistent disagreement/nuance:
* Open vs closed. 2,8,3,4,11,10 still emphasize GC directly secures the open, variable-governed schema Fx and a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx], generality with respect to the singular mode of presentation m of a. The unrestricted ∀x Fx is a world-involving claim about the extension of F; Fa + GC gives no information about other objects. Hence in the strong substantive sense GC does not require understanding/acceptance of ∀x Fx.
* Terminology split: “understand” = be able to entertain/parses given concept possession + quantifier mastery vs “understand” = be in a position to assess truth/warrant. The former gives Yes, the latter gives No.
* Colleague 2’s point about generality with respect to m vs generality with respect to F remains live: possession of F is separate from the requirement that m be deployable with any G. The canonical Evansian generalisation for the singular term is ∀x[x=a → Fx], not unrestricted ∀x Fx.

My current stance:
GC forces general possession of F, i.e. Fx with x free/arbitrary. With independent grasp of ∀ that general possession makes ∀x Fx intelligible/parses as the quantified articulation of the same F, so in intelligibility sense Yes. It does not give doxastic commitment, warrant or knowledge that ∀x Fx is true. The real substantive deliverable of GC is projectibility of F and the open schema / a-generalisation; closure under ∀ is a further step enabled by stipulated quantifier competence, not a further metaphysical commitment forced by GC.

Unresolved for me: whether Evans intended the intelligibility of the unrestricted universal to be just the trivial consequence of general possession + quantifier mastery, or whether he wanted to block even that intelligibility and keep GC limited to the open schema and a-generalisation. The discussion suggests the former is the dominant reading in this group, but the No camp’s insistence on the substantive/world-involving reading of ∀x Fx remains a tension to track.
reflection_text.4:
The deliberation is now converging on a qualified Yes / intelligibility answer, with the key variable being how “understand ∀x Fx” is read.

Shared background remains stable:
* GC is a constraint on concept possession / mode of presentation, not on truth, warrant or entailment Fa → ∀x Fx.
* To genuinely think/understand Fa, F must be possessed as a general, projectible concept, not an a-bound tag. Possession = ability to deploy F independently of a, i.e. to entertain the open schema ‘x is F’ / Fx for an arbitrary x, and to recombine F inferentially.

Division refined in round 1:
* Intelligibility-Yes camp (1,4,5,7,8,12,13,14,10,11,6,3). They now mostly accept the nuanced formulation: GC secures the open schema Fx and the general grasp of F. With the stipulated mastery of universal quantification, the conceptual resources for the closed form ∀x Fx are already in place. Understanding Fa therefore commits you to being able to entertain/parse/grasp the content of ∀x Fx as a meaningful proposition about F, even though you have no warrant, knowledge or doxastic commitment that ∀x Fx is true.
* Nuanced No / only open-schema / a-generalisation camp (2,3,10,11,8). They stress that GC per se secures projectibility of F, i.e. Fx with x free/arbitrary, and the a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx]. The closed, world-involving claim ∀x Fx is not entailed and does not require semantic commitment; at most you can syntactically form it because you independently understand ∀. The essential deliverable is generalisability, not endorsement of the universal.

Points of agreement emerging clearly:
* No one holds GC entails Fa ⊨ ∀x Fx as truth or gives epistemic warrant.
* GC does give a general grasp of F, so Fx for arbitrary x is required.
* Disagreement is now largely terminological: does “being able to understand ∀x Fx” mean being able to parse/entertain the quantified content given F+∀, or does it mean being committed to the substantive universal claim? The former is widely allowed; the latter is rejected.

My current working synthesis:
GC requires the open, generalisable deployment of F, i.e. ability to think Fx for arbitrary x. That, together with stipulated understanding of universal quantification, makes the sentence ∀x Fx intelligible/parsable and entertainable as a content built from the same generally possessed F. It does not make you committed to its truth, nor does Fa give warrant for ∀x Fx. The essential requirement secured by GC is the schema / general concept, not the endorsement of the universal generalisation. The a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx] is the canonical expression of generality with respect to the singular term a; possession of F is expressed as the ability to think Fx for arbitrary x.

Unresolved for later rounds:
* Precise wording of the question: “understand Fx (\forall x)” can be read as the open schema vs the closed universal. I need to keep both readings distinct and make explicit which sense of ‘understand’ is intended – intelligibility/possession vs doxastic commitment/knowledge of extension.
* Whether the Yes camp’s move from open schema + ∀ competence to intelligibility of ∀x Fx is a trivial syntactic closure or a substantive Evansian systematicity claim. Colleague 2 maintains even intelligibility of the unrestricted universal is not required, only a-generalisation.

Earlier material still relevant: GC is about systematicity and projectibility, singular thought is posterior to general concept, and possession of F is possession as a type available for recombination.
reflection_text.3:
The discussion has converged on core Evansian distinctions and the remaining dispute is now narrowly about intelligibility vs commitment and open schema vs closed universal.

Core agreement preserved from round 0:
* GC is a constraint on concept possession / mode of presentation and systematicity, not on truth, belief or warrant. Fa → ∀x Fx is not an entailment.
* To genuinely think Fa one must possess F as general/recombinable, not as a token tied to a. That requires being able to entertain the open schema ‘x is F’ for an arbitrary x, substitute different terms, combine with other concepts, etc.
* Intelligibility/possession is distinct from warrant/belief. GC secures projectibility of F, not knowledge of its extension.

Round 1 refinement:
* Yes/intelligibility camp now explicitly frames the Yes as intelligibility/possession not doxastic commitment. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,3,4,5,6,7,9 now say: given stipulated mastery of ∀, possession of F as general is possession of the material for ∀x Fx; understanding ∀ is understanding closure of an open formula, so Fa + quantifier competence makes ∀x Fx entertainable/parsing-able as a meaningful content about F. The singular thought is posterior to the general concept, and with ∀ in hand the general concept is manifest as the universal form. Colleague 10,11,12,4,6 stress this is intelligibility, not warrant.
* No/only-schema camp remains with Colleagues 2,8 and nuanced 3,4,6: GC secures the free-variable schema Fx and the a-generalisation ∀x[x=a→Fx], i.e. generality with respect to the singular mode of presentation of a and projectibility of F. The closed universal ∀x Fx is a substantive world-involving claim about the extension of F. GC gives no information about other objects and does not require grasp of the truth-conditions/commitment to the universal. Syntactic formability of ∀x Fx follows only from independent quantifier competence, not from GC.
* Colleague 2’s focus persists: generality required is with respect to m/a, giving ∀x[x=a→Fx], not unrestricted ∀x Fx.

Unresolved for me:
* The question phrasing “understand Fx (\forall x)?” is ambiguous. If “understand” = have F in general form i.e. entertain Fx with free x, answer is clearly yes by GC. If “understand” = be able to entertain the closed substantive proposition ∀x Fx as a content, the round shows a near-consensus that you can parse/entertain it given quantifier mastery, but a minority insists GC does not secure semantic understanding of that closed claim, only the open schema.

No change in prior belief yet; I am tracking the narrowing to intelligibility yes / commitment no, with the open vs closed tension still live.
reflection_text.10:
The question is about what Evans’ Generality Constraint plus stipulated competence with ∀ commits you to when you understand Fa: formal intelligibility/parsing of ∀x Fx vs substantive commitment to/warrant for the universal claim.

Core Evansian point stable: to think/understand Fa singularly you must possess F as a general, recombinable concept, not token-tied to a. Possession = ability to deploy F in the open schema Fx with x free/arbitrary, substitute terms salva conceptu, combine inferentially. GC is a constraint on concept possession/format of entertainability, not a logical entailment Fa → ∀x Fx and not a claim about truth/warrant.

Round 1 convergence:
- Yes-leaning in intelligibility sense: 1,10,11,12,13,14,4,5,6,7,9. They argue singular thought is posterior to general concept. Once F is possessed generally and ∀ is assumed understood, the closed form ∀x Fx is the quantified articulation of the same general mode of presentation. Understanding ∀ is understanding closure of an open formula; with general F you can entertain ∀x Fx as a meaningful content, parse it and know what it says, even without warrant/belief/knowledge that it is true.
- No/qualified No holding out: 2,3,8. They stress GC secures projectibility of F and generality w.r.t. the singular term a, i.e. the a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx] and the open schema Fx for arbitrary x, not the unrestricted substantive proposition ∀x Fx about the extension of F. They allow syntactic formability given ∀ competence, but deny that GC requires semantic understanding/commitment to the universal generalisation.

Common ground retained:
- GC does not give warrant, knowledge or belief that ∀x Fx is true; no inference from instance to universal.
- No one claims GC entails truth of ∀x Fx.
- Stipulated quantifier competence is essential; without it you only get open schema.

Unresolved nuance that drives disagreement:
- Is “able to understand ∀x Fx” meant as: can parse/form it with same concept F once ∀ is mastered, or can fully grasp its truth conditions/accept it as content? The former is now widely conceded; the latter is disputed.
- Distinction between generality w.r.t. F vs generality w.r.t. the singular mode of presentation m/a. Colleague 2’s a-generalisation is repeatedly invoked as the canonical GC deliverable for singular terms, with unrestricted ∀x Fx being a further world-involving commitment GC is silent about.
- Parsing vs semantic understanding: colleagues 10,11,12,6 distinguish ability to entertain ∀x Fx as intelligible propositional form from being able to assess its truth value.

Current leaning remains the qualified position: GC gives you general F and hence the open schema Fx, and with assumed ∀-competence the formal intelligibility/possession of ∀x Fx. GC does not require you to understand/accept the substantive universal claim about all objects being F, nor to have epistemic warrant for it. The remaining tension is whether that formal intelligibility counts as “being able to understand ∀x Fx” on Evans’ account, and whether the open schema is sufficient or the unrestricted closure is mandated.
reflection_text.12:
The question is whether, given GC and assumed competence with ∀, understanding Fa suffices for understanding ∀x Fx, where “understand” is about conceptual possession/intelligibility not warrant/truth.

Round 1 and Round 2 show convergence on two points and persistent divergence on one.

Convergent points:
- GC is a constraint on concept possession / format of entertaining thoughts, not a licence to infer Fa → ∀x Fx or to be warranted/believe that ∀x Fx is true.
- To think/understand Fa on Evans you must possess F as a general, projectible mode of presentation not essentially tied to a. Possession of F is the ability to deploy F independently of a, i.e. to entertain the open schema Fx with x free/arbitrary, to substitute salva conceptu, to form x=a→Fx, ∃x Fx, etc.
- Fa is intelligible only against the background of that general grasp of F. Singular thought is posterior to the general concept.

Divergence remains about the step from general possession + quantifier competence to the closed universal ∀x Fx.

Yes / intelligibility camp – 1,10,11,12,13,14,5,6,7,9: General possession of F is the only conceptual ingredient needed for a quantified thought with F as matrix. With ∀ already mastered, possessing F generally just is possessing the resources to entertain the quantified articulation of F. Understanding ∀ is understanding the rule by which an open formula Fx is closed. So Fa plus GC commits you to Fx for arbitrary x, and with quantifier competence that background is manifest as the ability to entertain ∀x Fx as a meaningful content, to know what it would say to ascribe F to every x. This is intelligibility/parsability, not belief or knowledge that ∀x Fx is true. Colleague 10 now explicitly says yes in intelligibility/possession sense, no in epistemic commitment sense; 11,12,13,14 make the same qualification.

No / schema-only camp – 2,3,4,8: GC secures projectibility / free-variable entertainability of F, i.e. Fx with x free and the a-generalisation ∀x[x=a→Fx]. ∀x Fx is a substantive, world-involving claim about the extension of F. Understanding Fa gives you a general concept F and a fact about a, no information about other objects. With ∀ competence you can syntactically form ∀x Fx, but GC does not require semantic understanding/acceptance of the closed universal as content. The constraint is about generality with respect to the singular mode of presentation of a and generality of the predicate as schema, not about commitment to the unrestricted generalisation.

Key distinctions now sharpened:
- General concept possession vs truth commitment / warrant. All agree GC gives the former not the latter.
- Free-variable schema Fx vs closed universal ∀x Fx. Most Yes camp identify them once ∀ is mastered; No camp insists GC delivers only the former.
- Generality with respect to F vs generality with respect to a. Colleague 2 stresses Evans’ singular-term generality: GC requires you can think m is G for every G you possess, and the canonical formal expression is ∀x[x=a→Fx], not ∀x Fx. Others treat predicate generality as the core.

Unresolved for me: the wording of the target. If the question means “understand the open schema Fx with a free variable”, consensus is essentially unanimous – GC requires it. If it means “understand the closed proposition ∀x Fx as substantive content”, the debate is whether intelligibility automatically follows from general possession + ∀ competence. The No camp’s intuition is that understanding the sentence is not the same as understanding the claim about the extension; the Yes camp’s intuition is that for a quantifier-competent thinker grasp of the schema and grasp of ∀ just is grasp of ∀x Fx, modulo no commitment to its truth.

I keep the central locus as ability to form/parse vs being committed to content/truth, and the a-generalisation vs unrestricted universal distinction as the place where the disagreement lives. Earlier round split of Yes 1,4,5,7,8,13,14 vs No 10,11,2,3,6 has narrowed: 10,11 now endorse the intelligibility reading, leaving 2,3,4,8 as the persistent no-on-closed-universal holdouts.
reflection_text.8:
Evans Generality Constraint is a constraint on concept possession / format of thought, not a licence for Fa → ∀x Fx or for warrant/belief in the universal.

Core agreement preserved: to think/understand Fa you must possess F as a general, projectible mode of presentation, not a token-tied tag to a. Possession = ability to deploy F independently of a, i.e. to entertain the schema `x is F` / Fx with x free/arbitrary, substitute terms, combine inferentially, etc. Singular employment presupposes general employment; Fa is intelligible only against background of a general grasp of F.

Disagreement in round 1 is mostly terminological about the closed universal vs the open schema, and about what “understand ∀x Fx” means.

Pro-intelligibility/possession reading, now largely held by colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,4,5,6,7,9: GC secures generalisability of F. With the stipulation that universal quantification is understood, general possession of F = conceptual resources to close the open schema under ∀. Possessing F generally together with grasp of ∀ gives competence to parse/entertain ∀x Fx as a meaningful proposition whose matrix is the same F used in Fa; you can know what it would say to ascribe F to every x, entertain ∃x Fx, etc. That is intelligibility/parsing/systematicity, not epistemic commitment, warrant, knowledge or truth of ∀x Fx. Fa does not entail ∀x Fx, GC does not give information about F-status of other objects.

Pro-limitation / open-schema-only reading, colleagues 2,3,8 and partly 10/11/12 in their strong sense: GC secures only the open, variable-governed schema Fx and the a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx]; generality is with respect to the singular mode of presentation a / m, not an unrestricted claim about extension of F. Understanding Fa gives you general concept F and fact about a, no information about others. With quantifier competence you can syntactically form ∀x Fx, but GC does not demand semantic understanding or acceptance of the substantive closed claim that every object is F. The closed universal is a world-involving claim about extension; GC secures projectibility, not truth.

Synthesis I am maintaining: GC requires the general schema Fx. With stipulated ∀-competence the sentence ∀x Fx is in principle intelligible as the quantified articulation of that same general concept. The weak sense - ability to entertain/parse the content - yes; the strong sense - doxastic commitment, entailment, warrant that ∀x Fx is true - no.

Unresolved phrasing issue: the question shorthand “Fx (\forall x)” conflates open schema with closed universal. Need to keep both the open-schema requirement Evans demands and the closed-form intelligibility that follows once ∀ is mastered, while explicitly denying entailment to truth/belief. The a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx] remains the canonical Evansian formalisation of generality with respect to a.

reflection_text.6:
The Evansian core is stable: to think/understand Fa you must possess F as a general, recombinable mode of presentation, not a token-reflexive tag tied essentially to a. Possession of F is possession of the ability to deploy F independently of a, i.e. to entertain the open schema Fx for an arbitrary x, to substitute terms for the argument place, and to combine F inferentially. Singular thought is posterior to general concept.

Round 1 largely converges on the intelligibility/warrant distinction that was already flagged. GC is a constraint on concept possession and the format in which a thought can be entertained, not a principle of inference Fa → ∀x Fx and not a source of warrant, knowledge or belief that F holds of everything. Understanding Fa gives you a general concept F and a fact about a; it gives no information about the F-status of other objects.

The current split is therefore verbal about what counts as “understanding ∀x Fx”.

Yes/intelligibility camp 1,10,11,12,13,14,5,6,7,9: General possession of F plus stipulated mastery of ∀ makes the closed form intelligible/parasable. Possessing F generally just is possessing the resources to embed Fx under the quantifier you already grasp. Understanding ∀ is understanding the rule that closes an open formula; with quantifier competence in hand the open schema Fx is systematically closable, so ∀x Fx is the same general mode of presentation exhibited in quantificational form. They stress this is possession/intelligibility, not endorsement: GC does not give warrant for, nor commitment to, the truth of ∀x Fx, and does not license inference from Fa to ∀x Fx.

No/open-schema camp 2,8 with nuance from 3,4,6: GC secures projectibility/free-variable entertainability of F, i.e. Fx with x free and, canonically, the a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx], generality with respect to the singular mode of presentation of a. The unrestricted closed universal ∀x Fx is a substantive world-involving claim about the extension of F. Understanding Fa gives you the general concept F and the ability to form the string ∀x Fx syntactically once ∀ is mastered, but GC does not require you to grasp, assess or be committed to the substantive content that every object is F. The requirement is for the schema, not the endorsement of the universal generalisation.

Persistent unresolved nuances:
* Intelligibility/ability to entertain vs warrant/belief/truth of ∀x Fx.
* Open schema Fx with free variable vs closed universal ∀x Fx.
* Generality with respect to the concept F vs generality with respect to the singular term a/m, i.e. a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx] vs unrestricted ∀x Fx.
* GC as condition on possession vs logical entailment Fa → ∀x Fx.

My working synthesis remains: GC requires possession of F in general form, i.e. ability to think Fx for an arbitrary x. Given stipulated quantifier competence, that general possession makes ∀x Fx intelligible as a meaningful content you can entertain with the same mode of presentation of F used in Fa. GC does not entail belief, knowledge or epistemic warrant for ∀x Fx, nor does it license Fa → ∀x Fx. The remaining disagreement is largely how much weight to give the open/closed distinction once ∀ is assumed mastered, and whether Evans’ canonical generality is better captured by the a-generalisation rather than the unrestricted universal.
reflection_text.2:
The debate has converged around a nuanced distinction between intelligibility/possession and warrant/belief/truth.

The Generality Constraint is now widely described as a constraint on concept possession and on the format in which a thought can be entertained, not a principle of inference Fa → ∀x Fx and not a commitment to the truth or extension of F. To understand / think Fa on Evans is to possess F as a general, projectible, recombinable mode of presentation, not a tag essentially tied to a. Possession of F is possession of the open, variable-governed schema x is F, ability to substitute different terms for the argument place, to form conditionals, negations, etc. with F, and in particular to entertain the a-generalisation ∀x[x = a → Fx], x = a → G(a), etc. That is generality with respect to the concept F and, in Colleague 2’s formulation, generality with respect to the singular mode of presentation of a.

With that in place the dispute is whether, given the stipulation that I understand universal quantification, that general possession already yields intelligibility of the closed universal ∀x Fx.

Yes/intelligibility camp – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,4,5,6,7,9 – argue that understanding ∀ is understanding the operation of closing an open formula over a domain. General possession of F is the matrix for ∀x Fx. Once F is possessed as the schema Fx and ∀ is mastered, the closed form ∀x Fx is the same general mode of presentation made explicit by the quantificational apparatus. In that Evansian sense of being able to entertain a content, parse it, know what it would say to ascribe F to every x, understanding Fa commits me to being able to understand ∀x Fx as a meaningful thought about F, even though I may be agnostic about its truth. The particular instance is posterior to the general concept; systematicity requires that Fa be intelligible only against the background of a generally available F, and with ∀ in hand that background is manifest as the intelligibility of the universal form. No warrant, knowledge or belief that ∀x Fx is true is required.

No/nuanced camp – Colleagues 2,3,8, and parts of 10/11/4 – stress that GC secures only projectibility/free-variable entertainability, i.e. Fx with x free/arbitrary, and the a-generalisation ∀x[x = a → Fx]. Understanding Fa gives me a general concept F and a fact about a, but no information about the F-status of other objects and no semantic grasp of the truth-conditions of the substantive closed proposition ∀x Fx. That the string ∀x Fx can be syntactically formed from a generally possessed F plus mastered ∀ is trivial parsing competence, not the semantic understanding of the universal claim that every object is F. The substantive claim remains world-involving and is not entailed nor required by GC; GC is about the generality of the mode of presentation of F and of the singular term a, not an unrestricted claim about the extension of F.

Key distinctions I am retaining:
* open schema Fx with free/arbitrary variable vs closed quantified proposition ∀x Fx;
* intelligibility/possession/parsing vs doxastic commitment, warrant, knowledge of truth;
* generality with respect to predicate F vs generality with respect to singular term a / mode of presentation m, hence the canonical Evansian generalisation is the a-generalisation not the unrestricted universal.

Changes from earlier: I now see broad convergence that GC does not give epistemic commitment to ∀x Fx and does not licence Fa ⊢ ∀x Fx. The remaining live issue is the strength of the ‘understand ∀’ stipulation. If understanding ∀ is really understanding closure, then possession of the open schema plus ∀ competence arguably yields intelligibility of ∀x Fx as content. If understanding ∀ is taken more minimally, GC only requires the open projectible form.

Unresolved for me: whether Evans himself requires grasp of the unrestricted closed universal as a thought, or only the projectible open schema and a-generalisation. The textual emphasis on projectibility and singular-term generality points toward the latter, while the systematicity and ‘possession = ability to recombine with quantifiers’ line points toward the former in the weak intelligibility sense.

I agree with 10, 11, 12, 14 and 3 on where the weight of the Generality Constraint actually lies, and I think 2 and 8 are drawing a parsing distinction that evaporates once quantificational competence is stipulated.

GC is about possession format, not about warrant or truth. To understand Fa in Evans’ sense is to possess F as a general mode of presentation, not as a tag glued to a. Possession of F just is the ability to deploy F independently of a, i.e. to entertain the schema x is F for an arbitrary x, to substitute salva conceptu, to combine F with negation, conditionals, etc. That is the projectibility the Constraint secures.

That general possession is the only conceptual ingredient of a universally quantified thought with F as matrix. The stipulation that you understand universal quantification is not a stipulation that you can form the string ∀x Fx. It is a stipulation that you grasp the rule by which an open formula is closed under ∀, that you know what it is to say ‘for every x’, and what it would be for a content to fall within the scope of that operator.

Given that, the ability to entertain Fx for an arbitrary x and the ability to understand ∀x Fx are not two different abilities. The open schema is quantifier-ready precisely because F is possessed as a type. Closing it under ∀ does not introduce a new mode of presentation of F; it exhibits the same general mode of presentation you were already required to have for Fa to be intelligible at all. In Evansian terms understanding is the ability to entertain a content on the basis of concept possession, not the ability to assess its truth, nor a commitment to believe it.

2 is right to stress that Fa gives you no information about the F-status of other objects and that GC does not licence Fa → ∀x Fx. That is uncontroversial and no one is claiming epistemic entitlement or doxastic commitment. What 2 calls ‘semantic understanding of ∀x Fx as the claim that every object is F’ is just a description of what the quantifier does. Once you grasp ∀, entertaining the closed form is exactly what it is to know what the thought says.

The a-generalisation ∀x[x=a → Fx] that 2 and 8 highlight is the canonical expression of generality with respect to the singular term a. It is perfectly intelligible, and it is intelligible for the same reason ∀x Fx is intelligible: you possess F generally and you possess ∀. Treating the restricted generalisation as a deep difference and the unrestricted one as a substantive world-involving commitment is to treat quantifier competence as syntactic only, which is precisely what the stipulation rules out.

So yes, in the Evansian intelligibility/possession sense: understanding Fa commits you, by GC, to a general grasp of F, and with an independent grasp of ∀ that general grasp is manifest as the competence to understand ∀x Fx as a meaningful proposition about F, even while you remain entirely agnostic about its truth.
